'''Alfred Washington Hales''' (born November 30, 1938) is an American mathematician, a professor emeritus of mathematics at the [[University of California, Los Angeles]], and one of the namesakes of the [[Hales–Jewett theorem]]. He was born in [[Pasadena, California]], and is the older brother of [[R. Stanton Hales]].<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=B687AAAAMAAJ&q=%22Hales,+alfred+washington%22+1938|title = Who's who in Frontier Science and Technology|year = 1984| publisher=Marquis Who's Who |isbn = 9780837957012}}</ref>

==Professional career==
As an undergraduate, Hales was a two-time [[William Lowell Putnam Mathematical Competition|Putnam Fellow]] for the [[California Institute of Technology]], in 1958 and 1959.<ref>[http://www.maa.org/awards/putnam.html The Mathematical Association of America's William Lowell Putnam Competition] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20000229230334/http://www.maa.org/awards/putnam.html |date=2000-02-29 }}, retrieved 2013-01-21.</ref> Hales stayed at Caltech for his graduate studies, earning his Ph.D. in 1962 under the supervision of [[Robert P. Dilworth]].<ref>{{mathgenealogy|name=Alfred Washington Hales|id=10406}}</ref> He is the former chair of the mathematics department at UCLA, and in 2010 became chair of the board of trustees of the Institute for Pure and Applied Mathematics at UCLA.<ref name="ipam">Al Hales Chairs IPAM Board of Trustees, [http://www.ipam.ucla.edu/news.aspx IPAM News & Announcements] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130118052342/http://www.ipam.ucla.edu/news.aspx |date=2013-01-18 }}, July 15, 2010, retrieved 2013-01-21.</ref>  From 1992 to 2003, he was director of the [[Institute for Defense Analyses#Center for Communications and Computing|IDA Center for Communications Research]] in La Jolla, California.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Hales|first1=Alfred|title=Sol Golomb--my friend and mentor|journal=Asia Pacific Mathematics Newsletter|pages=30–35|date=December 2017|volume=7|issue=1|url=http://www.asiapacific-mathnews.com/07/0701/0030_0031.pdf|access-date=June 14, 2023}}</ref>

==Contributions==
In 1963, Hales and [[Robert I. Jewett|Jewett]] published the [[Hales–Jewett theorem]], which is a standard part of [[Ramsey theory]] now. They motivated their theorem as a form of [[game theory]]: it shows that certain high-dimensional generalizations of [[tic tac toe]] cannot have any tied positions.

Hales also contributed to [[Solomon W. Golomb]]'s highly cited work on [[shift register]]s,<ref>[http://www.jmargolin.com/sense/refs/ref14_golomb.pdf Shift Register Sequences], [[Solomon W. Golomb]] with portions co-authored by Lloyd R. Welch, Richard M. Goldstein, and Alfred W. Hales, Aegean Park Press, 1982.</ref> and he has been noted for his work using [[Height (abelian group)|Ulm invariants]] to characterize infinite [[abelian group]]s.<ref name="ucla-aaas"/>

==Awards and honors==
In 1971, Hales shared the [[George Pólya Prize]] with [[Ronald Graham]], Klaus Leeb, [[Bruce Lee Rothschild]], and [[Robert I. Jewett]], for their work in [[Ramsey theory]].<ref>[http://www-history.mcs.st-and.ac.uk/Societies/SIAMPolyaPrize.html The George Pólya Prize], [[MacTutor History of Mathematics archive]], retrieved 2013-01-21.</ref> In 2009, Hales was elected a [[Fellow of the AAAS]],<ref name="ucla-aaas">[http://newsroom.ucla.edu/portal/ucla/PRN-5-ucla-professors-selected-fellows-149946.aspx 6 UCLA professors named fellows by American Association for the Advancement of Science] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100701175259/http://newsroom.ucla.edu/portal/ucla/PRN-5-ucla-professors-selected-fellows-149946.aspx |date=2010-07-01 }}, Stuart Wolpert, UCLA, December 17, 2009, retrieved 2013-01-21.</ref> and in 2013 he became a fellow of the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref>[https://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list List of Fellows of the American Mathematical Society], retrieved 2013-01-21.</ref>
